questions.q: In Problem 3 (committee selection), why is computing the complement (1 - P(no women)) the faster approach for "at least 1 woman"?
options: The complement method is actually slower and should be avoided
Complement methods only work when probabilities are exactly 50%
This problem cannot be solved using combinatorics at all
Computing P(no women) directly requires one calculation, versus summing P(exactly 1) + P(exactly 2) + P(exactly 3) + P(exactly 4) separately for the direct approach
questions.explain: "At least 1" is a classic signal to compute the complement -- it collapses four separate calculations into one, which is exactly the efficiency an interviewer is watching for.

questions.q: In Problem 4 (Bayesian signal reasoning), why is 70% (the signal's accuracy on up days) NOT the answer to "given the signal says up, what's the probability the market is actually up"?
options: The base rate (55% of days are up anyway) and the signal's down-day accuracy both have to enter the calculation via Bayes' theorem -- the raw accuracy-on-up-days figure alone ignores false positives from down days
70% actually is the correct final answer
Bayes' theorem is not applicable to trading signal problems
The signal's down-day accuracy is irrelevant to this calculation
questions.explain: Mistaking the signal's own stated accuracy for the posterior probability is the most common error in this style of problem -- the full Bayes' theorem calculation, including the base rate and false-positive rate, gives a different (here, ~81%) answer.

questions.q: In Problem 5 (market entry game), why does the payoff matrix have TWO Nash equilibria instead of one?
options: A payoff matrix can never have more than one Nash equilibrium, so this is an error

Neither firm has a dominant strategy -- the best move for each firm depends entirely on what the other firm does, so (Enter, Don't Enter) and (Don't Enter, Enter) are both stable outcomes where neither firm wants to unilaterally switch
Neither firm entering is also a Nash equilibrium in this game
Both firms entering is also a Nash equilibrium in this game
questions.explain: This game has a genuinely different structure from the Prisoner's Dilemma -- without a dominant strategy, multiple equilibria can coexist, and which one occurs is a coordination question the payoff matrix alone can't resolve.

questions.q: Why does this lesson instruct you to write down WHERE you got stuck and WHY, rather than just moving on when a problem is hard?
options: Writing down where you got stuck has no practical value
Getting stuck should never happen if you've studied the earlier lessons correctly
That information is exactly what you'd say out loud in a real interview rather than sitting in silence, and it's useful for identifying which earlier lesson to revisit
This instruction only applies to the hardest problem (Problem 5)
questions.explain: Articulating the specific point of confusion mirrors real interview behavior (narrating your reasoning, even when stuck) and gives you actionable information about which concept needs review.

questions.q: What is the lesson's stated reason for presenting these problems without worked examples shown first, unlike every other lesson in the course?
options: Students are expected to already know all five answers before starting
This lesson is identical in structure to every other lesson in the course
Worked examples are factually incorrect and were removed for accuracy reasons

A real quant interview gives you a problem cold with no worked example to pattern-match against -- you have to produce the reasoning yourself in real time, which reading a worked solution first doesn't practice
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly names this as the gap it's designed to close: every other lesson teaches by narrating a solution, which is a different skill from producing one yourself under real conditions.
